```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96)
```

VITROB assesses the risk of bias in one specified result from an in vitro
experiment. Reviewers answer signalling questions in six domains; the
package applies the published algorithms to propose a judgment for each
domain (Low, Some concerns or High) and overall, checks the answers for
entry errors, and draws the standard figures.

```{r}
library(vitrob)
```

## 1. Record the assessments

Write an empty entry sheet, one row per assessed result:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_template("my_assessments.csv")
```

An Excel version with drop-down answers and the full question text is
installed with the package:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
system.file("extdata", "assessment_template.xlsx", package = "vitrob")
```

Answer each signalling question with `Y`, `PY`, `PN`, `N` or `NI`, and leave
a question blank when its "asked if" condition is not met.
`questions_table()` lists every question with its condition, guidance and
references:

```{r}
q <- questions_table()
head(q[, c("domain", "id", "short", "ask_if")])
```

## 2. Read and check them

This vignette uses the 12 fictional results bundled with the package.

```{r}
ex <- read_assessments(system.file("extdata", "example_assessments.csv",
                                   package = "vitrob"))
check_assessments(ex)
```

`check_assessments()` lists invalid codes, missing required answers,
answers to questions that should have been skipped, overrides without a
reason and inconsistent overall judgments. An empty result means no
problems were found.

## 3. Proposed judgments

```{r}
res <- propose_judgments(ex)
res[, c("study_id", paste0("D", 1:6, "_proposed"), "overall_proposed")]
```

Assessors can override a proposed judgment by entering a different one in
the `<domain>_final` column with a reason in `<domain>_reason`; the plots
use the final judgment where one is given.

A single result can also be assessed directly from a named vector of
answers:

```{r}
propose_domain("D1", c("1.1" = "Y", "1.3" = "N"))
```

## 4. Figures

Traffic-light plot, one row per result:

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
plot_traffic(ex)
```

Share of judgments in each domain (pass `weight` for meta-analysis weights):

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_summary(ex)
```

Every signalling-question answer, coloured by whether it points towards low
or high risk:

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
plot_questions(ex)
```

Where primary studies most often fail to report (share of "No information"
answers per question):

```{r, fig.height = 5}
plot_gaps(ex)
```

The default colours are blue, amber and red, which remain distinguishable
with the common forms of colour-vision deficiency; `palette = "cochrane"`
gives green, amber and red. Every judgment also has a symbol (+, −, ×).

Save a figure at journal resolution with a height that fits the number of
rows:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
save_rob_plot(plot_traffic(ex), "traffic_light.png")
save_rob_plot(plot_traffic(ex), "traffic_light.pdf")
```

## 5. Point-and-click app

Reviewers who do not use R can upload a filled CSV or Excel sheet, see the
checks, judgments and figures, and download them:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_app()
```

## 6. Checking the algorithms

`verify_algorithms()` enumerates every valid combination of answers in every
domain and confirms that the rules never propose Low and High together, that
every judgment is reachable, that a worse answer never gives a better
judgment, and that every question can change the judgment.

```{r}
v <- verify_algorithms()
v[, c("domain", "profiles", "passed")]
```
